facts.statehood_note: Admitted as a slave state under the Missouri Compromise of 1820. The capital moved from St. Charles to Jefferson City in 1826.
facts.nickname: The Show Me State (unofficial; Missouri has no official nickname. It is also called the Cave State and the Gateway to the West.)
facts.motto: Salus populi suprema lex esto (Latin: Let the welfare of the people be the supreme law)
facts.name_origin: Named for the Missouri River, which was named for the Missouria people, a Siouan-speaking nation. French colonists borrowed an Illinois-language name for them, Wimihsoorita, meaning 'one who has dugout canoes.'

government.chambers: Missouri Senate (34 members, 4-year terms) and Missouri House of Representatives (163 members, 2-year terms); senators may serve two terms and representatives four terms, 8 years in each chamber
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; no one may be elected governor more than twice). The governor appoints the heads of executive departments with the consent of the Senate.
government.courts: Supreme Court of Missouri (7 judges), meeting in Jefferson City. Under the Missouri Nonpartisan Court Plan, approved by voters in 1940, a commission nominates three candidates, the governor picks one, and voters later decide whether to keep the judge.
government.local: 114 counties plus the independent city of St. Louis, which is not part of any county.
government.constitution: Missouri's fourth and current constitution was adopted in 1945. The first (1820) allowed slavery and tried to keep free Black people out of the state; the 1865 constitution abolished slavery.
government.kid_line: "That all political power is vested in and derived from the people; that all government of right originates from the people, is founded upon their will only, and is instituted solely for the good of the whole." (Article I, Section 1)

long_ago.about: The Osage moved west from the Ohio River valley and by the 1600s lived near the Osage River in western Missouri. They farmed, hunted buffalo, and by the early 1800s were the strongest power in the region, with a main village near the Osage River.

The Missouria broke away from related peoples in the Great Lakes region and by the late 1600s lived near where the Grand River meets the Missouri River. Their name became the name of the river and the state.

Before 1000 CE, Mississippian peoples built towns with large earthen mounds at present-day St. Louis and at nearby Cahokia in Illinois, trading from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico. St. Louis was once called 'Mound City' for its many mounds.
The Sauk and Meskwaki (Fox) held lands in northeastern Missouri, which they gave up in the Treaty of St. Louis.

first_peoples.today_note: Missouri has no federally recognized tribes today. Nations whose homelands include Missouri were forced out and now have governments elsewhere, such as the Osage Nation and the Otoe-Missouria Tribe, both in Oklahoma.
sites: Fort Osage, near Sibley, where the Osage signed the 1808 Treaty of Fort Clark
St. Louis, once called 'Mound City' for its Mississippian mounds, across the river from the Cahokia mound center

history.event: People are living along Missouri's river valleys; they have lived there continuously ever since.
Mississippian peoples build mound towns at present-day St. Louis and Cahokia; the culture declines by about 1400.
The Osage settle near the Osage River and the Missouria near the Missouri and Grand Rivers.
French Canadians found Ste. Genevieve, the first European settlement in Missouri. Early Missouri settlements depend on enslaved Africans and Native Americans for farm and fur-trade work.
French fur traders found St. Louis on February 14; it becomes the center of the fur trade.
The United States buys Missouri in the Louisiana Purchase, and the Lewis and Clark Expedition starts up the Missouri River from St. Charles.
In the Treaty of Fort Clark, Osage chiefs give up their lands east of Fort Osage in Missouri and Arkansas to the United States.
Four powerful New Madrid earthquakes shake the Bootheel region of southeastern Missouri.
On August 10, Missouri becomes the 24th state, entering as a slave state under the Missouri Compromise.
After conflicts over religion and slavery, Governor Lilburn Boggs issues an 'Extermination Order,' and Mormon settlers are violently driven out of Missouri.
Dred and Harriet Scott sue for freedom in St. Louis. In 1857 the U.S. Supreme Court rules against them, a decision that deepens the conflict leading to the Civil War.
On May 21, Mary Meachum helps freedom seekers cross the Mississippi River to Illinois and is arrested; the site is now the Mary Meachum Freedom Crossing.

A state convention votes against secession, but Missouri ends up with rival governments and is torn apart by battles such as Wilson's Creek and by guerrilla warfare. In January 1865 Missouri abolishes slavery, and a new constitution is ratified on June 6, 1865.
Black Union veterans of the 62nd Colored Infantry raise money to found Lincoln University in Jefferson City, Missouri's first Black university.

trailblazers.name: White Hair (Pawhuska)
trailblazers.text: White Hair claimed to be head chief of all the Osage, whose villages were in western Missouri. In 1804 he traveled to Washington, D.C., where President Thomas Jefferson recognized him as head chief, though many Osage did not accept a single chief. In 1808 he signed a treaty giving up most of the Osage homeland in Missouri and Arkansas to the United States, which cost him the trust of many Osage.

trailblazers.name: John Berry Meachum
trailblazers.text: He founded the First African Baptist Church in St. Louis and taught Black students in its basement when that was illegal. When Missouri banned education for Black people, he started the Floating Freedom School on a steamboat on the Mississippi River.

trailblazers.name: Mary Meachum
trailblazers.text: With her husband John, she helped freedom seekers on the Underground Railroad. On May 21, 1855, she helped a group cross the Mississippi River to Illinois and was arrested; the Mary Meachum Freedom Crossing was the first Missouri site in the National Park Service's Underground Railroad Network to Freedom.

trailblazers.name: Dred Scott
trailblazers.text: Enslaved in St. Louis, he and his wife Harriet sued for their family's freedom because they had lived where slavery was illegal. The Supreme Court ruled against them in 1857, but the family was freed by private arrangement that May.

trailblazers.name: Elizabeth Keckley
trailblazers.text: Born into slavery, she became a skilled dressmaker and in 1855 bought freedom for herself and her son in St. Louis. She later became dressmaker to First Lady Mary Todd Lincoln and started a relief group for formerly enslaved people during the Civil War.

trailblazers.name: George Washington Carver
trailblazers.text: Born into slavery on Moses Carver's farm near Diamond, Missouri, he became a leading agricultural scientist at Tuskegee Institute. He taught poor farmers to grow peanuts and sweet potatoes to restore soil worn out by cotton.

trailblazers.name: Annie Turnbo Malone
trailblazers.years: 1869–1957 (some records give her birth year as 1877)
trailblazers.text: Born in Metropolis, Illinois, she built a business in St. Louis making and selling hair products for Black women, selling door to door when stores would not carry her products. In 1918 she founded Poro College, which trained Black women in cosmetology. She gave away most of her money to charity, and the St. Louis Colored Orphans Home was renamed for her in 1946.

landforms: Karst land with sinkholes and more than 7,300 caves
geography.regions: Rolling glaciated plains north of the Missouri River, the Ozark Plateau with caves and springs in the south, and the flat, fertile Bootheel lowlands in the southeast.

ecosystems.name: Ozark springs and rivers
ecosystems.about: Giant springs pour billions of gallons of cold water into the Current and Jacks Fork Rivers each week, and at least 38 animal species live only in Ozark springs and underground waters.

ecosystems.name: Caves
ecosystems.about: Missouri has more than 7,300 recorded caves, second only to Tennessee; Perry County has the most.

ecosystems.name: Oak-hickory forest
ecosystems.about: South of the Missouri River, oak-hickory hardwood forest covers much of the land, including the Mark Twain National Forest.

ecosystems.name: Prairie and plains
ecosystems.about: North of the Missouri River, rolling plains were once tallgrass prairie; big bluestem is the state grass.

science.weather: Cold winters and hot, humid summers, with extremes from −40°F to 118°F. Missouri is in Tornado Alley: an EF5 tornado on May 22, 2011, destroyed about a third of Joplin and killed more than 150 people. The New Madrid Seismic Zone in the Bootheel produced four huge earthquakes in 1811 and 1812.
science.resources: Farming, especially cotton and rice in the fertile Bootheel; mining, remembered in old nicknames like 'the Lead State' and 'the Iron Mountain State'; and brewing and wine started by German immigrants. Today Missouri also has major companies in health care, finance, and manufacturing.
science.highlight: Ozark National Scenic Riverways was the first national park area created to protect a river system; its springs are among the largest in the world, and each one makes its own sound, from a roar to a soft splash.

g3_ss.title: Missouri Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Jefferson City, Kansas City, St. Louis, and the two big rivers, and learn what the General Assembly, governor, and Supreme Court do.

g3_ss.title: Missouri's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Learn about the Osage, the Missouria, and the mound builders of St. Louis, and where these nations live today.

g3_ss.title: Missouri Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Osage leader White Hair, John and Mary Meachum, Elizabeth Keckley, George Washington Carver, and Annie Turnbo Malone.

g45_ss.title: Missouri's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Study the Mississippian mound towns, Osage and Missouria homelands, and the 1808 Treaty of Fort Clark.

g45_ss.title: Fur Trade and the Gateway to the West
g45_ss.plan: Trace Ste. Genevieve, St. Louis, enslaved labor in early settlements, the Louisiana Purchase, and Lewis and Clark.

g45_ss.title: Missouri 1821–1877: Slavery, War, and Freedom
g45_ss.plan: Examine the Missouri Compromise, the Dred and Harriet Scott case, the Meachums, a divided Civil War, the end of slavery in 1865, and Lincoln University.

g3_sci.title: Caves of the Cave State
g3_sci.plan: Explore how water makes caves and sinkholes and meet cave animals.

g3_sci.title: Ozark Springs
g3_sci.plan: Learn where spring water comes from and why spring water stays cold all year.

g3_sci.title: Tornado Safety
g3_sci.plan: Learn how tornadoes form in Tornado Alley and how families stay safe.

g45_sci.title: The New Madrid Earthquakes
g45_sci.plan: Investigate faults, the 1811–1812 earthquakes, and earthquake safety.

g45_sci.title: Two Great Rivers
g45_sci.plan: Compare the Missouri and Mississippi Rivers, floods, and levees.

g45_sci.title: Saving the Hellbender
g45_sci.plan: Study the endangered hellbender salamander and what clean streams need.
